prize_parts.citation: For the magic-wavelength optical lattice clock, in which Katori's concept of trapping many neutral atoms free of Doppler, recoil and light-shift errors was developed by Ye and collaborators into clocks with 10^-18 accuracy and stability, enabling millimetre-scale tests of gravitational redshift and searches for variation of constants.

statement.case_for: I keep B049 as a single-part prize with Katori and Ye, and my preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1. After the full exchange the scientific case looks to me stronger, not weaker, because the dispute has narrowed to one question: is the lattice clock a new regime or a refinement of 2005 and 2012? As a theorist who works next to experiments on superconducting devices, I read it this way. The 2005 prize honoured the comb as a ruler for optical frequencies, and the 2012 prize honoured control of single quantum systems, with the single-ion clock as the example. The lattice clock changes the counting statistics: thousands of neutral atoms are interrogated at the same time, with the first-order Doppler and recoil shifts removed by Lamb-Dicke confinement, and the lattice light shift cancelled at the magic wavelength. That is a different physical design and not a better version of the ion clock. It gave stability that lets two clocks resolve a gravitational redshift across a millimetre, and a fractional uncertainty near 10^-18 that several laboratories have verified by comparison (JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE). It also lets the many-body physics of the atoms in the lattice show up directly in the clock, which is the kind of every-physical-detail control that I value. The two-name credit is cleaner than for any other shortlisted candidate. Reproducibility across laboratories is complete, and the physics does not wait on the SI redefinition. I also looked again at whether a second part is possible. B049 uses two names, so any second part could have only one person, and no member has proposed a one-name part that survives attribution scrutiny. I therefore see no coherent two-part option.
statement.case_against: The honest objection is the one that Danielsson, Eriksson and Mehlig press: so far the clocks have measured with great precision but have not yet found a result from nature that was unexpected, whereas twisted bilayer graphene opened a new route to strong correlation. There is also a real lineage question. The comb prize and single-ion clocks sit close by, Ye's laser-stabilisation work partly lies in recognised territory, and the priority history of the magic-wavelength idea and the lattice-clock demonstrations, including Lemonde and the SYRTE mercury work, Hollberg, Gill and NIST colleagues, is something I am recalling from memory and have not verified in the primary literature. I cannot rule out that a careful reading would require a wider credit than two names. If the committee decides that the discovery content is insufficient, I would accept B009 as the better alternative, because it has a clean theory-experiment structure, but I would still want the citation to avoid the pairing mechanism.

responses.point: Danielsson accepts the clean attribution of B049 but says the 2005 and 2012 prizes already cover the conceptual ground of laser metrology, and that he does not yet see a result from nature that changes how we think; he would rank it higher after a redefinition of the second or an anomalous result.
responses.response: I agree that no anomaly has appeared, and I would not claim one. But the test of a discovery in a precision field is whether it opens measurements that were not possible before, and the millimetre-scale redshift comparison is already one: it moves a textbook prediction of general relativity from kilometre-scale rocket and aircraft tests to a laboratory sample. The null results on constants are also real physics, as limits on the coupling of fundamental constants to gravity and to dark sector candidates. I do not think the committee should wait for a surprise or for the redefinition of the second. In my view neither the SI decision nor an anomaly would change what the lattice clock has already shown about how well time can be defined and compared. Your own statement that you keep it as a serious alternative is a fair position, and I would ask you to weigh the instrument case on those two grounds in the final vote.

responses.point: Mehlig argues that twisted bilayers revealed a previously unknown route to strong correlation, compares the open pairing glue to the cuprates at the time of recognition, and asks what essential new physical mechanism the lattice clock has, calling magic-wavelength trapping a clever way to cancel a systematic shift.
responses.response: The cuprate comparison is fair and it softens my maturity worry about B009, so I will say so openly. On the clock, I would resist calling the magic wavelength only a systematic cancellation. The point is that the clock states acquire the same ac Stark shift in a lattice for a specific wavelength, so one can confine atoms tightly enough to remove motional effects without paying with a shifted transition. This turned an unavoidable tradeoff into a free parameter and made a many-atom optical clock possible at all. That is a mechanism in the same sense as the quenching of kinetic energy in the moire problem, but it is a mechanism of measurement. I accept that you weigh a new state of matter above that, and the decision between B049 and B009 is largely a decision about that weighting. I do not think the maturity question favours B009: the clock has been reproduced by independent groups for fifteen years and the moire phase diagram for about seven.

responses.point: Olsson says the lattice clock question, distinct invention versus extension of 2005 and 2012, is a judgment on novelty that the committee should settle on the record and not on the shared Chalmers connection, and she adds that the 2025 prize makes B040 a hard sell, with Girvin missing from the names.
responses.response: I appreciate that, and I agree the record should decide. For the record, my case for B049 rests on the many-atom, Doppler- and recoil-free interrogation and on the verified redshift and stability results, none of which depends on my own field. On B040 I remain recused and I note that your attribution point about Girvin would be reason enough for me to keep it out of my final configuration even if I were not conflicted. I would also say, as a Chalmers colleague, that I am not defending the clock because a first-rate quantum-engineering result happens to be in a field that is close to mine. In terms of the physical regime, it is a different system from the superconducting circuits, and my confidence comes from the multi-laboratory agreement and not from a feeling of kinship.

responses.point: Eriksson argues that the open mechanism in twisted bilayer graphene is the normal state of a young field and no reason to postpone, and that the clock is the less surprising achievement, an extraordinary refinement of a known measurement principle.
responses.response: I agree that a young field with an open mechanism can still deserve a prize, and I have moved a little on this point since round 1: I no longer see the pairing question as a strong argument against B009 by itself. My remaining hesitation is attribution, since the Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto flat-band work and the experimental co-first authors cannot be handled inside three names. For the clock, I would call it a new measurement principle, not a known principle refined, because the many-atom magic-wavelength design is what allows the 10^-18 level. Still, I accept that you and I weigh surprise differently, and I would defer to you and Danielsson on whether the B009 prediction record is clean enough, as condensed matter is outside my own area.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, now prefers B049 largely on the judgment of the atomic-physics colleagues and notes that this limits his confidence; he asks that the citation be framed narrowly enough to avoid overlap with the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-trap prizes.
responses.response: I would not lean on my judgment or on Lindroth's alone, and I share your caution about counting support. What I can offer from a neighbouring field is that the lattice-clock claims are checked by clock-to-clock comparisons that do not depend on one team's interpretation, which is what I ask of any quantum device result. For the citation, I have tied it to the magic-wavelength lattice, to the many-atom Doppler- and recoil-free interrogation and to the 10^-18 performance with its consequences for gravitational redshift and constants. It does not mention combs or stabilised lasers, and it does not mention ions, so the recognised lineage is left out of the credit. I would welcome Lindroth correcting me on the priority history, since she can read that record better than I can.

uncertainties: Priority history of the lattice clock: the magic-wavelength proposal, the first lattice-clock demonstrations in Sr, Yb and Hg, and the roles of Katori, Ye, Lemonde, Hollberg, Gill and NIST colleagues. I have not checked the primary papers and rely on memory.
Whether the committee finally treats a precision-measurement result as a discovery about nature, or weighs it below a new phase of matter as Danielsson and Mehlig do.
Whether the open pairing mechanism and the earlier flat-band literature would, in the end, make B009 a safer choice than I currently judge; I defer to the condensed-matter members on this.
Whether a two-part prize could be defended, given that B049 uses two of the three permitted names.
statement.conflict_note: I direct WACQT and work in superconducting circuits, and I am close to groups behind B040 (Wallraff, Schoelkopf, Blais) and to Chalmers colleagues Delsing and Wilson, so I recuse myself from any decision on B040 and do not include it in my configuration. I share the Chalmers and Gothenburg environment with Olsson and Mehlig, with no specific collaboration that I know of, and this is not a reason for either of us to favour a candidate. I have no apparent connection to Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer, or the other credited names in B012, B026, B047, B010, B011 or B029 from the provided profile.
